gsea_enrichment_analysis.description: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) determines whether an a priori defined set of genes shows statistically significant, concordant differences between two biological states. Includes ORA (Over-Representation Analysis), standard GSEA, and ssGSEA (single-sample GSEA) variants.

database_selection.description: Which gene set database to use for enrichment testing

general_pathway_overview.when: First-pass analysis, cancer studies, or when you want a summary of well-defined biological states with reduced redundancy
general_pathway_overview.why: Hallmark gene sets are curated summaries with decreased redundancy. The collection contains 50 well-defined gene sets representing specific biological states or processes, reducing multiple-testing burden and providing clearer interpretations.

metabolic_and_signaling_pathways.when: Investigating specific metabolic or signaling pathway involvement
metabolic_and_signaling_pathways.why: KEGG provides curated pathway maps with metabolic and signaling pathway context. Reactome offers the most comprehensive manually curated pathway database (>2,600 pathways in humans). Use KEGG for metabolism-focused questions, Reactome for signaling and immune pathways.

biological_process_function.value_or_range: GO (MSigDB C5) - split into BP, MF, CC
biological_process_function.when: Exploring broad biological processes, molecular functions, or cellular compartments
biological_process_function.why: Gene Ontology provides the most comprehensive functional annotation. Use GO:BP for biological processes, GO:MF for molecular function, GO:CC for cellular localization. Be aware of redundancy in GO terms - use semantic similarity to reduce redundancy.

immunology_studies.when: Studying immune cell states, vaccination responses, or immunological perturbations
immunology_studies.why: C7 contains >5,000 gene sets representing immune cell types, states, and perturbations derived from microarray and RNA-seq studies of the immune system.

community_curated_pathways.when: When you need community-curated pathways that may be more up-to-date for niche biology areas
community_curated_pathways.why: WikiPathways is community-curated and often contains more specialized and recently updated pathways than KEGG, particularly for disease-specific pathways.

common_mistakes: Using all MSigDB collections simultaneously, inflating multiple testing burden
Not selecting databases based on the biological question - using GO when KEGG pathway maps would be more informative
Ignoring MSigDB version differences between analyses making results non-comparable

gene_set_size_min.description: Minimum number of genes in a gene set to be included in analysis

default_recommended.why: Gene sets with fewer than 10-15 genes can generate significant NES scores with just 2-3 genes, making normalization inaccurate. The default of 15 provides a good balance between sensitivity and statistical reliability.

targeted_small_sets.when: Investigating specific small pathways known to be biologically relevant (e.g., specific TF target sets)
targeted_small_sets.why: Some biologically meaningful gene sets (e.g., specific microRNA targets) contain fewer than 15 genes. Lowering to 10 allows their detection, but results should be interpreted cautiously.

common_mistakes: Setting min_size too low (<10), generating false positives from 1-2 genes driving enrichment
Not checking which gene sets were excluded due to size filtering

gene_set_size_max.description: Maximum number of genes in a gene set to be included in analysis

default_recommended.why: Very large gene sets (>500 genes) have inaccurate NES normalization and tend to reflect broad biological categories rather than specific pathways. They are also prone to false positives from inter-gene correlations.

broad_go_terms.when: Using GO gene sets which can be very large and hierarchically redundant
broad_go_terms.why: GO terms near the root of the ontology can contain thousands of genes and are rarely informative. Restricting max_size to 200-300 focuses on more specific, interpretable GO terms.

common_mistakes: Using max_size > 1000, which leads to uninformative results dominated by large generic GO terms
Not understanding that both relaxing and restricting max_size affect NES normalization

fdr_threshold.description: False Discovery Rate cutoff for significance

phenotype_permutation.when: Using phenotype permutation mode (recommended when >= 7 samples per group)
phenotype_permutation.why: The Broad Institute recommends FDR < 0.25 for phenotype permutation because the permutation approach is more conservative. With >30 gene sets tested, FDR < 0.25 is the standard threshold.

gene_set_permutation.when: Using gene set permutation mode (used when fewer than 7 samples per group)
gene_set_permutation.why: Gene set permutation does not preserve inter-gene correlations, making the test more liberal. A stricter FDR threshold of 0.05 compensates for this.

robust_data_stringent.when: Large datasets with high statistical power, or for publication-quality results
robust_data_stringent.why: For robust datasets with many replicates, stricter thresholds increase confidence in reported pathways. Use FDR < 0.05 or even < 0.01 when powered to do so.

common_mistakes: Using FDR < 0.05 with phenotype permutation mode and concluding nothing is significant - the standard is 0.25 for this mode
Reporting nominal p-values instead of FDR-corrected q-values
Not reporting the permutation method used alongside the FDR threshold

method_selection.description: Choice between ORA, GSEA, and ssGSEA methods

ranked_gene_list_two_groups.when: You have differential expression results with a ranking metric (logFC, t-statistic, signed -log10 p-value) and a two-group comparison
ranked_gene_list_two_groups.why: GSEA uses the full ranked list, not just significant genes, making it more powerful than ORA. It detects coordinated changes in gene sets even when individual genes are not significant. Consistently among top-performing methods in benchmarks.

gene_list_only.when: You only have a list of significant genes (e.g., from clustering, no ranking available)
gene_list_only.why: ORA is the only appropriate method when you lack gene-level ranking. Simple, fast, and widely understood. However, it discards information about genes that didn't make the significance cutoff.

per_sample_scores.when: You need pathway activity scores for individual samples (e.g., for clustering, survival analysis, or patient stratification)
per_sample_scores.why: ssGSEA computes enrichment scores for each sample independently, enabling per-sample pathway activity comparison. Essential for applications where group comparisons are not the goal.

common_mistakes: Using ORA after differential expression when GSEA would be more appropriate and powerful
Applying an arbitrary p-value cutoff to create a gene list for ORA, discarding sub-threshold but biologically meaningful genes
Not specifying the correct background gene universe for ORA (must match your experimental platform)

background_genes.description: The gene universe used as baseline for enrichment testing (critical for ORA)

rna_seq_experiment.value_or_range: All expressed genes (e.g., CPM > 1 in at least N samples)
rna_seq_experiment.when: RNA-seq differential expression followed by ORA
rna_seq_experiment.why: Without limiting background to expressed genes, tissue-specific gene sets can appear enriched simply because tissue-specific genes are absent from non-expressed genes. The background should represent 'any gene that COULD HAVE been positive'.

microarray_experiment.value_or_range: All probes/genes present on the array
microarray_experiment.why: The array design determines which genes are detectable. Using all human genes as background when only a subset is on the array inflates enrichment statistics.

common_mistakes: Using default 'all genes in genome' as background for ORA instead of experiment-specific expressed genes
Using different background gene sets when comparing ORA results across experiments
Not filtering background to expressed genes, causing enrichment of tissue-specific gene sets as artifacts

ribosome_spliceosome_enrichment.description: Enrichment of ribosome, spliceosome, or proteasome pathways is extremely common and often artifactual
ribosome_spliceosome_enrichment.when_artifact: These pathways show up in nearly every differential expression analysis because ribosomal and spliceosomal genes are: (1) ubiquitously expressed at high levels, (2) internally correlated (co-expressed), and (3) sensitive to any perturbation affecting transcription or translation. Artifacts from gene-gene expression correlation cause false enrichment of these large, internally correlated gene sets.
ribosome_spliceosome_enrichment.when_real: Ribosome enrichment is biologically real in: translation regulation studies, mTOR pathway perturbations, ribosomal biogenesis disorders (Diamond-Blackfan anemia), stress responses (selective translation), and cancer (ribosome biogenesis upregulation). Spliceosome enrichment is real in: splicing factor mutations (e.g., SF3B1, U2AF1 in MDS/AML), neurodegenerative diseases with splicing dysfunction.
ribosome_spliceosome_enrichment.how_to_distinguish: 1) Check if enrichment is driven by consistent directional change or random correlation. 2) Examine leading edge genes - are they the same across all comparisons? 3) Use ssGSEA to check if enrichment score actually differs between groups at the sample level. 4) Compare against appropriate controls. 5) If ribosomal genes appear in EVERY comparison, they are likely artifacts.

gsea_enrichment_analysis.best_practice_notes: Always use hypothesis-driven database selection rather than testing all collections. For RNA-seq, prefer GSEA over ORA. Report the database version, permutation method, and FDR threshold. For ORA, always specify the background gene universe as expressed genes, not all genes. Watch for ribosome/spliceosome artifacts in every analysis.

chip_seq_peak_calling_macs2.description: MACS2 (Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq) identifies enriched regions (peaks) in ChIP-seq data by modeling the shift size of sequenced tags and using a dynamic Poisson distribution to capture local biases. It supports both narrow (point-source) and broad (dispersed) peak calling.

peak_type.description: Whether to call narrow or broad peaks, determined by the biological target

transcription_factors.when: ChIP-seq for transcription factors (TFs), co-activators, mediator, or any point-source binding factor
transcription_factors.why: TFs bind specific short DNA sequences, creating sharp, narrow peaks typically 100-300 bp wide. The default narrow peak calling mode with model building is optimized for these.

active_histone_marks.value_or_range: Narrow peaks for H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1; or broad with --broad for H3K4me1
active_histone_marks.when: ChIP-seq for activating histone modifications at promoters/enhancers
active_histone_marks.why: H3K4me3 and H3K27ac typically produce sharp peaks at promoters and enhancers. H3K4me1 marks enhancers and can be either narrow or moderately broad. Use narrow calling for H3K4me3/H3K27ac; consider broad for H3K4me1 depending on context.

repressive_histone_marks.when: ChIP-seq for H3K27me3, H3K9me3, H3K36me3, or any dispersed histone modification
repressive_histone_marks.why: Repressive marks cover broad genomic domains (10-100 kb). MACS2 broad mode performs 2-level peak calling: identifying stronger enriched regions within broader enriched domains. The --broad-cutoff controls the q-value for the broad region calling.

common_mistakes: Calling narrow peaks for H3K27me3/H3K9me3, missing the broad domains entirely
Using --broad for transcription factor ChIP-seq, creating falsely merged peaks
Not distinguishing between H3K4me3 (narrow) and H3K4me1 (can be broader)

q_value_vs_p_value.description: Statistical threshold for peak significance (mutually exclusive parameters)

standard_narrow_peaks.when: Standard TF or sharp histone mark ChIP-seq with good signal-to-noise
standard_narrow_peaks.why: Q-value (BH-corrected FDR) of 0.01 provides a good balance between sensitivity and specificity for narrow peaks. More stringent than the default -q 0.05.

standard_broad_peaks.why: Broad peaks have lower signal amplitude, requiring a more relaxed threshold. The --broad-cutoff separately controls the outer (broad) region calling while -q controls the inner (strong) region calling.

idr_workflow.when: Using the ENCODE IDR (Irreproducible Discovery Rate) framework with biological replicates
idr_workflow.why: IDR requires a relaxed initial peak calling threshold to provide enough peaks for reproducibility analysis. Use p-value 1e-3 to call a large set of peaks, then IDR filters to the reproducible set.

common_mistakes: Using both -p and -q simultaneously (they are mutually exclusive)
Relaxing -q threshold and not realizing it also makes peaks wider, not just more numerous
Not using IDR framework when biological replicates are available

atac_seq_parameters.description: Specific MACS2 parameter combinations for ATAC-seq data

paired_end_full_fragments.when: Paired-end ATAC-seq data where you want to use actual fragment sizes for pileup
paired_end_full_fragments.why: BAMPE format uses the actual insert size from paired reads to build fragment pileup. This is the general-purpose approach for ATAC-seq, preserving nucleosome-related fragment information. Note: --shift and --extsize are ignored in BAMPE mode.

cutting_site_focused.when: You want to focus on Tn5 transposase cutting sites for maximum resolution of open chromatin
cutting_site_focused.why: This shifts reads to center on the Tn5 cut site and extends 200bp, amplifying the cutting site enrichment signal. Provides the sharpest peaks at open chromatin regions.

encode_style.when: Following ENCODE project standards for ATAC-seq analysis
encode_style.why: Based on MNase-seq studies showing 75bp fragment centered on cutting site gives better resolution of nucleosome-free regions. Uses half-nucleosome fragment size.

common_mistakes: Using --shift and --extsize with BAMPE format (they are silently ignored)
Not using --nomodel for ATAC-seq when in single-end mode
Forgetting --keep-dup all for ATAC-seq (Tn5 can create genuine duplicate insertions at highly accessible sites)
Not adjusting for Tn5 insertion offset (+4/-5 bp adjustment for the 9bp duplication)

input_control.description: Whether and how to use input/IgG control for normalization

chip_seq_standard.value_or_range: Always use matched input control (-c input.bam)
chip_seq_standard.when: Any ChIP-seq experiment with available input control
chip_seq_standard.why: Input control corrects for: (1) open chromatin bias from sonication, (2) mappability bias, (3) copy number variations, (4) GC content bias. Without input, false positive peaks appear in highly accessible or amplified regions.

atac_seq.why: ATAC-seq measures open chromatin directly without immunoprecipitation. There is no appropriate input control. MACS2 uses a local lambda background model instead.

no_control_available.value_or_range: Use --nolambda to disable local background estimation, or proceed without control with increased caution
no_control_available.why: Without control, MACS2 uses a local Poisson model to estimate background. Results will have more false positives. Consider using --nolambda to use a uniform background instead.

common_mistakes: Using IgG control from a different cell type or condition than the IP sample
Not sequencing input to sufficient depth (should be at least equal to IP depth)
Using input control for ATAC-seq (not appropriate)

sequencing_depth.description: Minimum sequencing depth for reliable peak calling

transcription_factors.value_or_range: >=20 million uniquely mapped reads per replicate
transcription_factors.when: Point-source/narrow peak ChIP-seq for transcription factors
transcription_factors.why: ENCODE standards recommend >= 10M reads as minimum, with 20M as target for mammalian TF ChIP-seq. TFs have thousands of binding sites; sufficient depth ensures detection of weaker binding events.

narrow_histone_marks.why: ENCODE4 standards specify 20M usable fragments for narrow-peak histone experiments.

broad_histone_marks.why: Broad marks cover larger genomic regions and have lower signal amplitude, requiring more reads to distinguish enrichment from background. ENCODE4 specifies 45M usable fragments for broad marks.

rna_pol2.when: ChIP-seq for factors with very many binding sites (RNA Pol II, cohesin, CTCF)
rna_pol2.why: Proteins with widespread binding across the genome (>50,000 sites for Pol II) need proportionally more reads for saturation.

common_mistakes: Using the same depth guidelines for broad marks as narrow marks
Not accounting for PCR duplicates when assessing effective depth (NRF > 0.9 recommended)
Comparing peak numbers between experiments with very different sequencing depths

paired_end_parameters.description: How to handle paired-end sequencing data in MACS2

chip_seq_paired_end.why: BAMPE mode uses actual fragment sizes from properly-paired reads instead of modeling the fragment size distribution. This is more accurate than single-end mode with --extsize. Only properly-paired read alignments are used.

single_end_with_known_fragment_size.when: Single-end ChIP-seq where fragment size is known from bioanalyzer or cross-correlation analysis
single_end_with_known_fragment_size.why: When model building is unreliable (e.g., low read count or broad marks), explicitly setting the fragment size from experimental measurements is more reliable.

common_mistakes: Not specifying --format BAMPE for paired-end data, causing MACS2 to treat reads as single-end
Using --extsize with BAMPE format (it is ignored)
Not filtering for properly-paired reads before MACS2 analysis

chip_seq_peak_calling_macs2.best_practice_notes: Always determine peak type (narrow vs broad) before analysis based on the target protein. Use matched input controls for ChIP-seq. For ENCODE-style analysis, use the IDR framework with relaxed p-value threshold. For ATAC-seq, choose between BAMPE (full fragments) and shift-based (cutting site focus) approaches based on your question. Always check library complexity metrics (NRF, PBC1, PBC2) before peak calling.

motif_enrichment_homer.description: HOMER (Hypergeometric Optimization of Motif EnRichment) performs differential motif discovery by comparing two sets of sequences and identifying regulatory elements enriched in one set relative to the other. Uses ZOOPS scoring coupled with hypergeometric enrichment calculations.

background_selection.description: Choice of background sequences for motif enrichment comparison

default_random_genomic.value_or_range: Auto-generated GC-matched random genomic regions (default behavior when no -bg specified)
default_random_genomic.when: Standard ChIP-seq or ATAC-seq peak motif analysis without specific background requirements
default_random_genomic.why: HOMER automatically selects random genomic sequences matched for GC content, which is critical because GC-rich regions (e.g., CpG islands at promoters) would otherwise bias motif discovery. This is the most common and generally appropriate approach.

custom_background_regions.when: When you want to compare enrichment between two specific peak sets (e.g., condition-specific peaks vs shared peaks, or gained vs lost peaks)
custom_background_regions.why: Custom backgrounds test whether motifs are differentially enriched between your target peaks and specific control peaks. Essential for comparative analyses like differential binding or condition-specific accessibility.

promoter_analysis.value_or_range: Use matched promoter regions as background or use findMotifs.pl with -bg flag for promoter sets
promoter_analysis.when: Analyzing promoter-associated peaks or differentially expressed gene promoters
promoter_analysis.why: Promoters have distinct GC composition compared to intergenic regions. Using random genomic background for promoter peaks would show CpG-related motifs as top hits rather than genuine TF binding motifs.

common_mistakes: Not using GC-matched background, leading to GC-content-related artifacts in top motifs
Using peaks from a completely different cell type as background when cell-type-specific chromatin differences dominate the comparison
Using too few background sequences relative to target sequences

motif_length.description: Length(s) of motifs to search for

default_comprehensive.why: The default combination of 8, 10, and 12 bp covers most known TF binding motifs. Most TFs bind 6-12 bp core motifs. Running all three lengths simultaneously allows HOMER to find the optimal representation.

short_motifs_bzip_ets.when: Searching for short motifs like bZIP (7-8bp), ETS (7-8bp), or basic HLH motifs
short_motifs_bzip_ets.why: Some TF families have compact binding motifs. Adding length 6 captures these. However, shorter motifs increase false positive rate.

longer_motifs_composite.when: Searching for composite motifs or cooperative binding elements
longer_motifs_composite.why: Some regulatory elements involve closely spaced binding sites for two TFs (e.g., AP-1:IRF composite elements). Longer motif lengths can capture these. WARNING: lengths > 12 may cause memory issues - reduce input sequence count if needed.

common_mistakes: Using only a single motif length, missing motifs of different sizes
Setting motif length > 12 without reducing input sequences, causing memory exhaustion
Not realizing that the optimal length depends on the TF family being studied

known_vs_de_novo.description: Whether to search for known database motifs or discover novel motifs de novo

both_recommended.value_or_range: Run both (HOMER does this by default)
both_recommended.why: HOMER automatically performs both known motif enrichment and de novo motif discovery in a single run. Known motifs test against a database of characterized TF binding profiles. De novo discovery can identify novel or variant motifs not in the database.

known_only.value_or_range: -nomotif (skip de novo) to speed up analysis
known_only.when: When you have a specific hypothesis about which TFs should be enriched and want quick results
known_only.why: De novo motif discovery is computationally expensive. If you only need to test for known TF binding, skipping de novo saves significant time.

de_novo_focused.value_or_range: Standard run with focus on de novo results
de_novo_focused.when: Studying novel regulatory regions, non-model organisms, or looking for previously uncharacterized motifs
de_novo_focused.why: Known motif databases are incomplete, especially for non-model organisms. De novo discovery is essential when exploring novel biology.

common_mistakes: Only looking at de novo results and ignoring known motif enrichment, which provides biological interpretation
Not recognizing that multiple known motif matches for the same TF family (e.g., JUN, FOS, BATF all matching AP-1) are expected, not independent findings
Interpreting de novo motifs without comparing them to known motif databases

region_size.description: Size of region around peaks to analyze (-size parameter)

default_200bp.why: 200bp centered on peak summit captures the primary binding site while limiting noise from flanking sequences. This is the default and works well for most TF analyses.

given_regions.when: Analyzing ATAC-seq peaks, broad histone marks, or specific regulatory regions of varying sizes
given_regions.why: Uses the actual coordinates from the input BED file rather than resizing. Important when peak sizes are biologically meaningful (e.g., nucleosome-free regions in ATAC-seq).

common_mistakes: Using too large a region size (e.g., 1000bp) for TF motif analysis, diluting the signal
Not using -size given for ATAC-seq peaks where region boundaries are informative

motif_enrichment_homer.best_practice_notes: HOMER automatically normalizes for GC content, which is critical for unbiased motif discovery. The default -len 8,10,12 and -size 200 work well for most TF ChIP-seq analyses. For ATAC-seq, use -size given. Always examine both known and de novo results. Watch for AP-1 family motifs appearing as multiple separate hits (JUN, FOS, BATF, ATF) - these represent a single biological finding.

scrna_seq_integration.description: Methods for integrating multiple single-cell RNA-seq datasets to remove batch effects while preserving biological variation. Major methods include Harmony (linear, fast), scVI (deep learning VAE), BBKNN (graph-based), and Scanorama (MNN-based).

method_selection.description: Which integration method to use based on data characteristics

simple_batch_correction.when: Simple batch effects (same tissue, same protocol, different sequencing runs), small to medium datasets (<100k cells), quick analysis needed
simple_batch_correction.why: Harmony is fast, memory-efficient (30-50x less memory than Scanorama/MNN at 125k cells), and consistently performs well for simple integration tasks. Robust to parameter choices. Runs in <1 hour even for large datasets.

complex_integration_large_datasets.when: Complex batch effects (different protocols, different tissues), large datasets (>100k cells), when downstream tasks need a generative model
complex_integration_large_datasets.why: scVI uses a deep generative model that jointly models batch effects and biological variation. Performs best for complex integration tasks. Provides uncertainty estimates and supports downstream differential expression. Scales to millions of cells.

complex_nested_batch_effects.when: Multiple nested batch variables (e.g., samples from different locations AND conditions), when robust handling of complex batch structure is needed
complex_nested_batch_effects.why: Scanorama tends to perform best in complex integration tasks with nested batch effects, showing robustness in handling both subtle biological variation and strong batch effects.

graph_based_fast_robust.when: When you need a fast, graph-based approach that modifies the k-nearest neighbor graph directly; when you don't need a corrected expression matrix
graph_based_fast_robust.why: BBKNN is computationally efficient and demonstrated consistently reliable performance even with millions of cells. More robust across runs compared to deep learning methods. However, it does NOT produce batch-corrected expression values, limiting some downstream analyses.

with_cell_type_labels.when: Cell identity labels are partially or fully known for reference data
with_cell_type_labels.why: When cell type labels are available, semi-supervised methods (scANVI) and supervised methods (scGen) consistently outperform unsupervised approaches by using label information to preserve biological structure during integration.

common_mistakes: Always using the same integration method without considering data characteristics
Using BBKNN when downstream analyses require corrected expression values
Not comparing multiple integration methods on the same data
Integrating data when batch effects are minimal and integration would only add noise

scvi_n_latent.description: Dimensionality of the latent space in scVI

default.when: Standard datasets with moderate cell type diversity
default.why: Default value that works well for most datasets. The latent space captures the main axes of biological variation.

complex_datasets.when: Datasets with many cell types, subtypes, or continuous trajectories
complex_datasets.why: Higher dimensionality allows the model to capture more subtle biological variation. Useful for atlases with dozens of cell types.

simple_datasets.when: Simple datasets with few distinct cell types
simple_datasets.why: Lower dimensionality prevents overfitting and provides cleaner separation of major cell types.

common_mistakes: Using n_latent > 50, which leads to overfitting
Not using scVI's autotune module to systematically evaluate different n_latent values
Setting n_latent too low for complex atlas-scale datasets

scvi_n_layers.description: Number of hidden layers in encoder and decoder neural networks

default_recommended.why: Hyperparameter tuning studies consistently retain architectures with a single hidden layer. One layer provides sufficient model capacity for most scRNA-seq datasets while avoiding overfitting.

large_complex_datasets.when: Atlas-scale datasets (>500k cells) with complex batch structure
large_complex_datasets.why: Two layers can capture more complex nonlinear relationships. However, diminishing returns beyond 2 layers for most biological datasets.

common_mistakes: Using 3+ layers without evidence of improvement, increasing training time and overfitting risk
Not adjusting training epochs when increasing model complexity

scvi_n_hidden.description: Number of nodes per hidden layer in scVI

default.why: Default value that balances model capacity and computational cost.

large_datasets.when: Large datasets (>100k cells) or datasets with many highly variable genes
large_datasets.why: Best hyperparameter tuning results often come from configurations with 256 hidden neurons for larger datasets, suggesting more capacity is beneficial when data supports it.

common_mistakes: Using 512+ hidden nodes for small datasets, leading to overfitting
Not using the scVI autotune module to search over [64, 128, 256]

harmony_theta.description: Diversity penalty parameter controlling the strength of batch correction

default.when: Standard batch correction with moderate batch effects
default.why: Default value (theta=2) provides moderate diversity penalty. Harmony was shown to be robust to the choice of theta across a wide range of values.

strong_batch_effects.when: Strong batch effects where batches clearly separate in PCA space even after standard correction
strong_batch_effects.why: Higher theta increases the diversity penalty exponentially, forcing more aggressive batch mixing. Use when default theta fails to adequately mix batches.

subtle_batch_effects.when: Subtle batch effects or when there is concern about overcorrection removing biological variation
subtle_batch_effects.why: Lower theta reduces the diversity penalty, preserving more of the original data structure. Use when biological differences between batches are expected and should be maintained.

no_correction_control.when: Testing whether batch correction is needed (negative control)
no_correction_control.why: theta=0 disables the diversity penalty entirely. Useful for comparing corrected vs uncorrected results.

common_mistakes: Not testing multiple theta values to find the right balance
Using very high theta (>5) which can overcorrect and remove biological variation
Not assessing overcorrection after integration

when_not_to_integrate.description: Situations where batch integration should NOT be performed

biological_differences_expected.when: Comparing different tissues, disease states, or experimental conditions where biological differences are the focus of the study
biological_differences_expected.why: Integration methods cannot distinguish batch effects from biological variation. Aggressive integration removes true biological signals. If your scientific question IS about differences between groups, integration will remove the signal you are trying to detect.

minimal_batch_effects.when: Batches overlap well in PCA space and clustering is not driven by batch identity
minimal_batch_effects.why: If batch effects are minimal, integration adds noise and computational complexity without benefit. Always visualize PCA colored by batch before deciding to integrate.

single_batch.when: All data comes from a single experimental batch
single_batch.why: There are no batch effects to correct. Running integration on single-batch data can introduce artifacts.

common_mistakes: Automatically integrating all multi-sample datasets without assessing whether batch effects exist
Treating biological condition (e.g., healthy vs disease) as a batch variable and correcting for it
Not visualizing data before and after integration to assess what was removed

overcorrection_detection.description: How to detect and assess overcorrection after batch integration

metrics_based_assessment.value_or_range: Use kBET, LISI, ASW (Average Silhouette Width), and ARI metrics together
metrics_based_assessment.when: After any integration, before proceeding with downstream analysis
metrics_based_assessment.why: kBET is the most sensitive measure of remaining batch effect. LISI measures both batch mixing and cell-type separation. ASW evaluates clustering quality. No single metric captures all aspects - use multiple metrics together. Note: kBET and LISI may NOT detect overcorrection; use RBET for overcorrection-aware evaluation.

biological_signs_of_overcorrection.value_or_range: Check for: (1) ribosomal genes as cluster markers, (2) overlapping markers between clusters, (3) absence of expected cell-type markers
biological_signs_of_overcorrection.why: If cluster-specific markers are dominated by ubiquitous genes (ribosomal), if markers overlap significantly between clusters, or if expected cell-type markers disappear, integration has likely removed biological signal.

common_mistakes: Only checking batch mixing metrics (LISI) without checking cell-type preservation
Assuming high batch mixing = good integration (it could be overcorrection)
Not comparing clustering before and after integration to identify lost biological structure

scrna_seq_integration.best_practice_notes: Always visualize data (PCA, UMAP) colored by batch BEFORE deciding to integrate. If batches overlap well, integration may not be needed. When integrating, try multiple methods and compare using kBET + LISI + ASW + ARI. Watch for overcorrection signs: ribosomal genes as top markers, disappearance of expected cell type markers. For scVI, use the autotune module. For Harmony, theta=2 is a good default but test a range. Never treat biological conditions as batch variables.

cell_type_annotation_scrnaseq.description: Methods for assigning cell type identities to clusters or individual cells in single-cell RNA-seq data. Approaches include marker-gene-based manual annotation, reference-based automated annotation (SingleR, CellTypist), and deep-learning-based methods (scArches).

well_characterized_tissue.value_or_range: CellTypist or SingleR with tissue-matched reference
well_characterized_tissue.when: Studying well-characterized tissues (PBMC, brain, lung) where reference atlases exist
well_characterized_tissue.why: Automated reference-based methods are fast, reproducible, and leverage expert-curated atlases. CellTypist provides pre-trained models for multiple organs in human and mouse. SingleR can differentiate highly similar cell types better than some alternatives.

novel_tissue_or_species.value_or_range: Manual marker-gene annotation + de novo clustering
novel_tissue_or_species.when: Studying poorly characterized tissues, non-model organisms, or expecting novel cell types
novel_tissue_or_species.why: No reference atlas exists, so automated methods will misclassify cells. Manual annotation using known marker genes, combined with differential expression between clusters, is the only reliable approach.

atlas_scale_annotation.when: Annotating large atlas-scale datasets (>500k cells) or mapping new data to existing atlases
atlas_scale_annotation.why: scArches enables efficient mapping of new datasets onto existing reference atlases using transfer learning. CellTypist's majority voting mode provides consensus annotation for large datasets.

immune_cells_specifically.value_or_range: CellTypist with Immune_All_Low (high resolution) or Immune_All_High (low resolution) models
immune_cells_specifically.when: Annotating immune cell types across tissues
immune_cells_specifically.why: CellTypist was specifically developed for immune cell characterization across tissues. The Immune_All_Low model covers 101 annotated cell types including rare subtypes collected from different tissues.

combined_approach_recommended.value_or_range: Use automated methods + manual verification of top markers
combined_approach_recommended.when: Any annotation task requiring publication-quality results
combined_approach_recommended.why: No single automated method is 100% accurate. The best approach combines computational tools for efficiency with manual review of cluster-specific markers for validation. Check that automated annotations agree with known marker gene expression patterns.

common_mistakes: Blindly trusting automated annotations without manual verification
Using a reference atlas from a different technology platform (e.g., training on Drop-seq, applying to 10X Chromium) without considering platform effects
Not checking whether the reference atlas contains all expected cell types present in the query data

minimum_cells_per_cluster.description: Minimum number of cells needed in a cluster for reliable annotation

standard_annotation.when: Standard cell type annotation with reasonable confidence
standard_annotation.why: Sufficient cells are needed to reliably detect marker gene expression and distinguish signal from noise in sparse scRNA-seq data. Differential expression for cluster markers requires adequate sample sizes.

rare_cell_detection.value_or_range: As low as 0.5% of total cells (may be 20-50 cells)
rare_cell_detection.when: Detecting rare cell populations using specialized methods (e.g., MultiK)
rare_cell_detection.why: Specialized methods like MultiK can accurately identify rare cell populations at 0.5% frequency. However, annotation confidence is lower and should be validated with additional markers or orthogonal methods.

differential_expression_reliability.value_or_range: >=25 cells per group for DE testing
differential_expression_reliability.when: Using differential expression to identify cluster markers
differential_expression_reliability.why: Statistical tests for DE require minimum sample sizes. With fewer than 25 cells, power to detect differentially expressed markers drops substantially, leading to unreliable annotation.

common_mistakes: Annotating clusters with <10 cells and treating the annotation as confident
Over-clustering data to create artificially small clusters, then struggling to annotate them
Not adjusting clustering resolution to avoid splitting real cell types into sub-clusters too small to annotate

novel_cell_type_handling.description: How to handle cells that don't match any known cell type in the reference

uncertainty_based_detection.value_or_range: Use methods with uncertainty/rejection capability (scEMAIL, CAMLU)
uncertainty_based_detection.when: When novel cell types are expected in the query data
uncertainty_based_detection.why: Most supervised annotation methods label all cells as known types, potentially masking novel populations. Methods like scEMAIL use uncertainty measurement and bimodality tests to judge whether new cell types are present. CAMLU selects informative features to identify novel cells.

two_pass_approach.value_or_range: First annotate with automated method, then identify unassigned/low-confidence cells for manual investigation
two_pass_approach.why: Automated methods provide annotations for known cell types. Low-confidence or unassigned cells can then be investigated manually for novel cell type markers using DE analysis against all other clusters.

common_mistakes: Force-labeling all cells with the closest known cell type, missing novel populations
Not setting confidence thresholds for automated annotations
Assuming all cells must belong to a known cell type

reference_atlas_selection.description: Choice of reference atlas for automated annotation

tissue_matched_atlas.value_or_range: Use tissue-specific atlas (e.g., Human Lung Cell Atlas for lung data)
tissue_matched_atlas.when: Analyzing a specific tissue with available tissue-specific reference
tissue_matched_atlas.why: Tissue-matched atlases provide the highest resolution cell type annotations because they include tissue-specific subtypes and were trained on similar data. CellTypist models trained on cross-dataset atlases (e.g., 14 lung datasets for Human Lung Cell Atlas) are more robust than single-dataset references.

pan_tissue_atlas.value_or_range: Use Tabula Sapiens, Human Cell Atlas, or CellTypist pan-tissue models
pan_tissue_atlas.when: Studying mixed tissues, dissociated tumors with stromal infiltration, or when tissue-specific atlas is unavailable
pan_tissue_atlas.why: Pan-tissue atlases cover broad cell type diversity across organs. Useful when multiple tissue types are mixed (e.g., tumor microenvironment) or for initial exploratory annotation.

common_mistakes: Using a pan-tissue atlas when a high-quality tissue-specific atlas is available (lower resolution)
Not checking if the reference atlas technology matches the query data technology
Using a mouse reference for human data (or vice versa) without proper ortholog mapping

cell_type_annotation_scrnaseq.best_practice_notes: Always combine automated annotation with manual verification of marker genes. Use tissue-matched reference atlases when available. Set confidence thresholds and investigate low-confidence cells for novel cell types. Check that the reference data technology matches your query data. For immune cells, CellTypist provides the most comprehensive pre-trained models. Report annotation confidence scores alongside cell type labels.

protein_language_models_esm2.description: ESM-2 is a protein language model family from Meta AI trained on evolutionary-scale protein sequence data. Models range from 8M to 15B parameters and produce per-residue and per-sequence embeddings useful for structure prediction, function annotation, variant effect prediction, and more.

model_size_selection.description: Which ESM-2 model variant to use based on task and computational resources

optimal_balance.when: Most downstream tasks where GPU resources are available
optimal_balance.why: The 650M model provides substantially better representation quality than smaller variants. Medium-sized models (650M) demonstrated consistently good performance, falling only slightly behind 15B despite being 23x smaller. Comparable performance to the 3B Prot-T5 model while being more parameter efficient. Validation perplexity 6.95 vs 10.33 for 8M.

resource_constrained.when: Limited GPU memory, need to process many sequences, or running on consumer GPUs
resource_constrained.why: The 150M model outperforms the 650M parameter ESM-1b on structure-based tasks while being much smaller. Good compromise between quality and compute. Validation perplexity 7.75.

cpu_only_deployment.when: CPU-only environments, real-time applications, or screening millions of sequences
cpu_only_deployment.why: 5-10x faster inference than 150M model. Suitable for large-scale screening where speed matters more than accuracy. Validation perplexity 10.33.

maximum_accuracy.when: When accuracy is paramount and computational resources are not limiting (e.g., academic cluster with A100/H100 GPUs)
maximum_accuracy.why: The 3B model provides the best balance at the high end. The 15B model is often impractical (cannot be fine-tuned even on H100 GPUs) and offers diminishing returns over 3B.

common_mistakes: Defaulting to the largest model (15B) without considering that 650M achieves nearly equivalent results at 23x lower cost
Using 8M for tasks requiring high sensitivity (e.g., variant effect prediction) where accuracy matters
Not benchmarking multiple model sizes on your specific task

layer_selection.description: Which transformer layer(s) to extract embeddings from

general_purpose.when: Most downstream tasks including variant effect prediction, function annotation
general_purpose.why: Across most datasets, the last layer is the most commonly top-performing layer. In cases where it's not the best, the penultimate layer performs slightly better, and the last layer has only marginally lower performance. The last layer is the most effective and straightforward choice.

protein_function_classification.value_or_range: Mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 20-33 in the 33-layer 650M model)
protein_function_classification.when: Kinase classification, enzyme function prediction, or tasks where functional domain information is critical
protein_function_classification.why: Mid-to-late transformer layers capture richer function-level and motif-level information than the last layer alone. Probing experiments showed that layers 20-33 boost ARI in unsupervised clustering by 32% and raise classification accuracy to 75.7% vs 70.2% for last-layer only.

sequence_level_representation.value_or_range: Mean pooling across all residue positions of the last layer
sequence_level_representation.when: When you need a single vector per protein sequence (classification, retrieval, clustering)
sequence_level_representation.why: Mean embeddings consistently perform well across datasets. ESM C 600M with mean embeddings offers an optimal balance between performance and efficiency for transfer learning in realistic biological applications.

common_mistakes: Using the first few layers which contain primarily positional/token information rather than semantic protein representations
Not considering task-specific layer selection when maximum performance matters
Concatenating all layers, creating unnecessarily large feature vectors without proportional accuracy gains

sequence_length.description: Maximum input sequence length and handling of long proteins

standard_proteins.when: Most proteins (median human protein is ~375 aa)
standard_proteins.why: Standard ESM-2 was trained with a maximum input size of 1,022 amino acids. Most proteins fall within this limit.

long_proteins.value_or_range: Use sliding window approach: segment into <=1,022 aa slices, average embeddings position-wise
long_proteins.when: Proteins longer than 1,022 amino acids (e.g., titin, dystrophin, mucins)
long_proteins.why: Extended architectures support up to 2,046 aa. For longer sequences, a sliding window technique segments the sequence into non-overlapping slices, with embeddings aggregated by averaging feature vectors position-wise.

common_mistakes: Truncating long proteins without implementing sliding window, losing C-terminal information
Not checking sequence length limits before batch processing, causing silent failures
Including non-standard amino acid characters without mapping them to standard tokens

fine_tuning_vs_feature_extraction.description: Whether to fine-tune the entire model or use frozen embeddings as features

feature_extraction.value_or_range: Freeze ESM-2, extract embeddings, train lightweight classifier on top
feature_extraction.when: Limited training data (<5,000 samples), limited GPU resources, or when rapid experimentation is needed
feature_extraction.why: Feature extraction is fast, requires minimal compute, and works well for many tasks. Useful when fine-tuning would overfit on small datasets.

full_fine_tuning.value_or_range: Fine-tune entire model on task-specific data
full_fine_tuning.when: Large labeled datasets (>5,000 samples), task requires learning new protein features, and GPU resources are available
full_fine_tuning.why: Performance is systematically higher under fine-tuning compared to feature extraction. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning almost always improves downstream predictions. However, requires significant compute (cannot fine-tune 15B even on H100 with LoRA).

parameter_efficient_fine_tuning.value_or_range: LoRA or adapter fine-tuning of ESM-2 650M
parameter_efficient_fine_tuning.when: Moderate labeled data, want fine-tuning benefits with reduced compute cost
parameter_efficient_fine_tuning.why: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning achieves similar improvements to full fine-tuning with up to 4.5-fold acceleration. Enables fine-tuning of larger models on consumer GPUs.

common_mistakes: Fine-tuning on very small datasets (<1,000 samples) and overfitting
Attempting to fine-tune ESM-2 15B or 3B without sufficient GPU memory
Not using early stopping and validation monitoring during fine-tuning

protein_language_models_esm2.best_practice_notes: ESM-2 650M is the sweet spot for most applications - nearly as accurate as 3B/15B at a fraction of the cost. Use last-layer mean-pooled embeddings as a strong default. Consider mid-to-late layers for function classification tasks. For production, feature extraction with a lightweight head is often sufficient. Fine-tune only when you have >5,000 labeled samples and the task demands it. Use LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of larger models.

crispr_guide_design.description: Design of single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) for CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, including on-target efficiency scoring, off-target risk assessment, and application-specific design rules for knockout, CRISPRi, and screening applications.

gc_content.description: GC content of the 20-nt spacer sequence

optimal_range.when: Designing guides for standard SpCas9 knockout
optimal_range.why: 97% of functional sgRNAs have GC content between 30-80%, with optimal efficiency at 40-70%. Too low GC (<30%) reduces binding stability of the guide:target duplex. Too high GC (>70%) increases off-target binding due to stable mismatched duplexes and can cause secondary structures in the guide RNA.

extended_acceptable.when: When no guides in the 40-70% range are available for a target region
extended_acceptable.why: The outer range remains functional but with reduced average efficiency. Prioritize other design features (position, sequence context) when GC content is suboptimal.

common_mistakes: Selecting guides with extreme GC content (<20% or >80%) without checking alternatives
Not considering that high GC content increases off-target binding stability
Treating GC content as the sole selection criterion when other features matter more

position_specific_nucleotides.description: Preferred nucleotides at specific positions in the 20-nt spacer

pam_proximal_preferences.value_or_range: Prefer G at position 20 (PAM-proximal), avoid C at position 20; prefer purines at position 19; prefer C at position 18 (cleavage site); avoid U/T at positions 17-20
pam_proximal_preferences.when: Ranking candidate guides by predicted on-target efficiency
pam_proximal_preferences.why: Position 20 (immediately adjacent to PAM) is the most critical: G is strongly preferred, C is strongly disfavored. Multiple Us in the PAM-proximal spacer cause low sgRNA expression from the U6 promoter (runs of U act as Pol III terminators). C at position 18 (the Cas9 cleavage site) is associated with higher cutting efficiency.

seed_region_considerations.value_or_range: The 8-14 nt PAM-proximal seed region (positions ~7-20) is critical for specificity; a highly sensitive core is at positions 4-7 upstream of PAM
seed_region_considerations.why: Single mismatches in the seed region (especially positions 4-7 from PAM) abolish cleavage at off-target sites. The seed region is where Cas9 initiates target DNA unwinding. Mismatches in the PAM-distal region are more tolerated.

common_mistakes: Ignoring position-specific preferences when multiple guides are available
Not checking for poly-T runs (TTTT) in the spacer which terminate U6 transcription
Treating all mismatch positions equally when evaluating off-target risk

guides_per_gene.description: Number of independent sgRNAs to design per target gene

knockout_standard.why: Multiple independent guides confirm that the phenotype is due to gene disruption rather than off-target effects. 3 guides enables redundant targeting of 98.8% of genes. Use at least 2 effective guides to claim a phenotype.

knockout_screen.value_or_range: 6 guides per gene (optimal); 3 minimum for compact libraries
knockout_screen.when: Genome-wide or focused CRISPR knockout screens
knockout_screen.why: 6 guides per gene provides the best trade-off for genome-wide screening performance. Compact library designs with 3 guides per gene enable screening with fewer cells while still covering 98.8% of genes.

crispri_screen.why: Dual-sgRNA library designs achieve 82% median knockdown, significantly outperforming single-sgRNA libraries. Ultra-compact libraries with 1-3 elements per gene are sufficient due to higher CRISPRi efficiency.

crispri_individual.value_or_range: 2-3 guides targeting within 500bp downstream of TSS
crispri_individual.why: CRISPRi guides must be positioned near the transcription start site (within -50 to +300 bp of TSS) for effective repression. Multiple guides confirm the knockdown is not position-dependent.

common_mistakes: Using only 1 guide for knockout and attributing all phenotypes to on-target effects
Not using sufficient guides per gene in screens, reducing statistical power
Placing CRISPRi guides far from the TSS where they are ineffective

off_target_scoring.description: Method for scoring off-target binding and cleavage risk

cfd_score.when: Comprehensive off-target evaluation, especially for therapeutic applications
cfd_score.why: CFD score uses position-specific mismatch weights that vary by nucleotide substitution type. Outperforms MIT score in predicting actual off-target cleavage. Considers that rG:dT mismatches are generally tolerated (89% active) while rC:dC mismatches are poorly tolerated (37% active).

mit_score.when: Quick screening with widely available tools (e.g., CRISPOR, Benchling)
mit_score.why: MIT score is an older, simpler model that uses position-dependent weights but does not differentiate mismatch types. Still useful for initial screening but less accurate than CFD for detailed off-target assessment.

common_mistakes: Only checking for perfectly matched off-target sites and ignoring 1-3 mismatch sites
Not considering RNA:DNA mismatch type (rG:dT tolerated vs rC:dC not tolerated) in off-target assessment
Ignoring off-targets in the seed region (positions 4-7 from PAM) which have the strongest impact on specificity

pam_variants.description: PAM sequence recognition and activity for different Cas9 variants

standard_spcas9_ngg.when: Standard genome editing with wild-type SpCas9
standard_spcas9_ngg.why: NGG is the canonical PAM with the highest cleavage efficiency. Should be the default choice when an NGG PAM is available at the target locus.

alternative_nga.value_or_range: NGA PAM - average efficiency ~16% (3x lower than NGG)
alternative_nga.when: When NGG PAM is not available at the desired cut site and NGA is the best alternative
alternative_nga.why: NGA is recognized by wild-type SpCas9 but with significantly reduced efficiency. Consider using engineered Cas9 variants (xCas9, SpCas9-NG) for better NGA recognition.

alternative_nag.value_or_range: NAG PAM - average efficiency ~4% (12x lower than NGG)
alternative_nag.when: Primarily relevant as a source of off-target activity, rarely used intentionally
alternative_nag.why: NAG PAMs support very low but detectable cleavage by wild-type SpCas9. Important to consider as off-target sites but not recommended for on-target design.

pam_flexible_variants.when: When the target site absolutely requires a non-NGG PAM and no redesign is possible
pam_flexible_variants.why: Engineered variants expand targetable sequence space but come with increased off-target activity. SpRY (near-PAMless) has the broadest targeting range but the highest off-target risk. Always validate with off-target analysis.

common_mistakes: Using NAG or NGA PAMs with wild-type SpCas9 and expecting NGG-level efficiency
Not considering NAG/NGA PAMs as potential off-target sites when evaluating guide specificity
Using PAM-flexible variants without increased off-target scrutiny

crispr_guide_design.best_practice_notes: Design 3-6 guides per gene and validate at least 2. Use CFD score over MIT score for off-target assessment. Check GC content (40-70%), avoid poly-T runs, prefer G at position 20. For screens, 6 guides per gene with 50x cell coverage is optimal. For CRISPRi, target within 500bp downstream of TSS. Always use NGG PAM when available; engineered PAM-flexible variants increase off-target risk. Validate on-target editing efficiency experimentally before large-scale experiments.

atac_seq_analysis.description: ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing) maps open chromatin regions genome-wide using Tn5 transposase. Analysis includes fragment size-based quality control, peak calling, differential accessibility, and integration with other epigenomic data.

fragment_size_filtering.description: Filtering fragments based on size to isolate nucleosome-free and nucleosome-bound fractions

nucleosome_free_regions.why: Fragments shorter than 147 bp (nucleosome footprint) represent DNA from nucleosome-free regions where Tn5 can insert on both sides of an accessible stretch. These fragments are enriched at TSSs and enhancers and represent the primary signal of interest for chromatin accessibility.

mononucleosome_fragments.when: Analyzing nucleosome positioning or phasing around regulatory elements
mononucleosome_fragments.why: Fragments spanning a single wrapped nucleosome (147 bp core + linker DNA) provide information about nucleosome occupancy. These are depleted at TSSs but show characteristic phasing flanking active promoters.

all_fragments.when: Standard peak calling for open chromatin regions
all_fragments.why: For general peak calling, using all fragments maximizes signal. Fragment size filtering is more relevant for nucleosome-specific analyses.

common_mistakes: Not checking fragment size distribution as a quality control step
Missing the expected nucleosome periodicity pattern (peaks at ~200, 400, 600 bp) which indicates failed ATAC-seq
Filtering to NFR only when total signal is needed for peak calling

tss_enrichment_score.description: Signal-to-noise metric measuring read enrichment at transcription start sites

bulk_atac_seq.why: TSS enrichment is the primary signal-to-noise measure for ATAC-seq. NFR fragments should pile up at active TSSs. Low TSS enrichment indicates poor Tn5 insertion specificity or excessive background.

single_cell_atac_seq.why: ArchR and Signac use TSS enrichment >= 4 as a default threshold for pass-filter cells. Cells with lower TSS enrichment are likely dead cells, empty droplets, or failed tagmentation.

common_mistakes: Not calculating TSS enrichment as a primary QC metric
Proceeding with analysis despite low TSS enrichment, leading to unreliable peak calls
Using different TSS enrichment calculation methods across experiments, making comparisons invalid

frip_score.description: Fraction of reads in peaks - proportion of total reads falling within called peaks

encode_standard.why: ENCODE recommends FRiP > 0.3. Lower FRiP indicates high background noise relative to signal. However, FRiP depends on peak calling parameters and the total number of peaks.

common_mistakes: Using FRiP as the sole quality metric without TSS enrichment
Comparing FRiP values across datasets with different peak calling parameters
Not realizing that FRiP is circular (more relaxed peak calling = higher FRiP)

single_cell_minimum_cells.description: Minimum cells and fragments for reliable scATAC-seq analysis

per_cell_fragment_threshold.value_or_range: >= 1,000 unique nuclear fragments per cell (minimum); >= 10,000-15,000 reads per cell (sequencing depth)
per_cell_fragment_threshold.why: scATAC-seq data is inherently sparse (maximum 2 reads per locus per cell). Cells with fewer than 1,000 unique fragments lack sufficient information for reliable clustering and annotation. 10-15k reads per cell ensures adequate coverage.

experiment_scale.value_or_range: >= 3,000 cells per sample for major cell type recovery; >= 5,000-10,000 for rare cell types
experiment_scale.when: Experimental design and cell number planning
experiment_scale.why: Benchmarking studies used 3,000 cells per sample to recover all major PBMC cell types. More cells improve resolution for rare populations and differential accessibility power.

peak_calling_pseudo_bulk.value_or_range: Aggregate cells per cluster into pseudo-bulk for peak calling; minimum ~100-500 cells per cluster
peak_calling_pseudo_bulk.why: Per-cell data is essentially binary and peaks cannot be called at single-cell level. Pseudo-bulk aggregation provides sufficient read depth for MACS2 peak calling. Clusters with very few cells produce unreliable peaks.

common_mistakes: Attempting to call peaks at the single-cell level
Not filtering cells by both fragment count AND TSS enrichment
Using too few cells per cluster for pseudo-bulk peak calling, leading to unreliable peaks

nucleosome_signal.description: Ratio of mononucleosome to nucleosome-free fragments

quality_threshold.why: High nucleosome signal indicates poor tagmentation or dead cells where DNA is wrapped around nucleosomes. A ratio < 4 ensures cells have adequate nucleosome-free fragments for accessibility analysis.

common_mistakes: Not filtering cells with high nucleosome signal, including dead/dying cells in analysis
Confusing nucleosome signal with TSS enrichment - both are needed

atac_seq_analysis.best_practice_notes: Fragment size distribution is the first quality check - verify nucleosome-free peak (<147bp) and mononucleosome peak (~200bp). TSS enrichment >= 5-7 for bulk, >= 4 per cell for scATAC. FRiP > 0.3 (ENCODE). For scATAC, filter cells by unique fragments (>1000), TSS enrichment (>4), and nucleosome signal (<4). Peak calling must be done on pseudo-bulk data. Use Tn5 offset correction (+4/-5 bp). For differential accessibility, account for technical covariates (fragment count, TSS enrichment).

tfbs_analysis_jaspar.description: Transcription Factor Binding Site (TFBS) prediction using Position Weight Matrices (PWMs) from the JASPAR database. Involves scanning genomic sequences with PWMs to identify potential TF binding sites, requiring careful selection of scoring thresholds and background models.

score_threshold.description: Minimum score for calling a predicted binding site

relative_score_threshold.value_or_range: Relative score >= 0.80 (80% of maximum possible score)
relative_score_threshold.when: Standard TFBS scanning for enrichment analysis or regulatory element identification
relative_score_threshold.why: JASPAR uses a relative score >= 0.80 as default. This threshold balances sensitivity and specificity. The relative score normalizes for motif length and information content, making it comparable across different motifs.

stringent_scanning.when: When specificity is more important than sensitivity (e.g., predicting functional binding sites)
stringent_scanning.why: Higher thresholds reduce false positives at the cost of missing weaker binding sites. Appropriate when predicting sites for experimental validation.

p_value_based.why: P-value accounts for the background sequence composition and motif-specific score distribution. Using both relative score AND p-value provides dual quality control. P-value alone can be misleading because different motifs have different score distributions.

common_mistakes: Using a fixed absolute score threshold across different motifs (unfair to short/low-information-content motifs)
Not using both relative score and p-value together for quality control
Setting thresholds too low and being overwhelmed by false positive predictions

background_model.description: Background nucleotide frequency model for PWM scoring

uniform_background.when: Quick analysis or when genome composition is unknown
uniform_background.why: Simplest model, does not require pre-computation. However, may be inaccurate for genomes with non-uniform base composition.

genome_specific.value_or_range: Genomic nucleotide frequencies (e.g., human: A/T ~0.29, G/C ~0.21)
genome_specific.when: Standard TFBS scanning in a specific genome
genome_specific.why: Using genome-specific background frequencies accounts for compositional bias. In AT-rich genomes, AT-rich motifs would appear more often by chance, and genome-specific background corrects for this.

region_specific.value_or_range: Nucleotide frequencies computed from the analyzed regions (e.g., promoter composition)
region_specific.when: Scanning specific genomic regions with distinct composition (e.g., CpG islands, enhancers)
region_specific.why: Promoters and CpG islands have very different GC content than intergenic regions. Using global genome frequencies as background for CpG island scanning would underestimate GC-rich motif occurrence by chance.

common_mistakes: Using uniform background for AT-rich or GC-rich genomes, biasing predictions
Not adjusting background when scanning promoters vs intergenic regions
Using whole-genome frequencies when only scanning a subset of regions with distinct composition

redundant_motif_handling.description: How to handle multiple similar motifs from the same TF family

jaspar_non_redundant_core.value_or_range: Use JASPAR CORE collection (non-redundant by design)
jaspar_non_redundant_core.why: JASPAR CORE is curated to be non-redundant, with different profiles for the same factor only when they recognize significantly different motifs. This reduces but doesn't eliminate redundancy from related TF family members.

post_hoc_clustering.value_or_range: Cluster similar motifs using TOMTOM or motif similarity metrics, report representative motifs
post_hoc_clustering.when: When scanning with all JASPAR motifs and getting many hits from the same TF family
post_hoc_clustering.why: Related TFs (e.g., multiple ETS family members) have similar binding preferences. Reporting all individually inflates the number of findings. Clustering by motif similarity and reporting the best match per cluster provides cleaner results.

common_mistakes: Reporting each TF family member as an independent finding when they share the same motif
Not using the CORE (non-redundant) collection and instead using all JASPAR profiles
Not clustering results by motif similarity for final reporting

species_specificity.description: Whether to use species-specific or cross-species motif profiles

same_species.value_or_range: Use species-specific profiles from JASPAR (vertebrates, plants, fungi, insects, urochordata, nematodes)
same_species.when: Analyzing a species with adequate representation in JASPAR
same_species.why: JASPAR CORE is divided by taxonomic groups. Species-specific profiles may capture lineage-specific binding preferences and are derived from experiments in the relevant organism.

cross_species_conservation.value_or_range: Use JASPAR phyloFACTS collection or vertebrate collection for cross-species comparisons
cross_species_conservation.when: Studying conserved regulatory elements across species or analyzing non-model organisms without species-specific profiles
cross_species_conservation.why: phyloFACTS contains motifs derived from evolutionarily conserved sequences across mammals (human, mouse, rat, dog). For non-model organisms, using vertebrate profiles from closely related species is the best available approach.

common_mistakes: Using human motifs for plant genome analysis without considering divergent TF binding preferences
Not checking if the TF of interest has species-specific profiles available in JASPAR
Assuming TF binding preferences are identical across all vertebrates

tfbs_analysis_jaspar.best_practice_notes: Use JASPAR CORE (non-redundant) collection with species-appropriate taxonomic group. Apply dual thresholds: relative score >= 0.80 AND p-value < 0.05. Match background model to the genomic context being scanned (promoter vs genome-wide). Cluster redundant motif hits from TF families. For cross-species work, use the phyloFACTS collection or the closest taxonomic group available. Always validate computationally predicted TFBSs with experimental evidence (ChIP-seq, footprinting).

genomic_coordinate_liftover.description: Converting genomic coordinates between different genome assemblies (e.g., hg19 to hg38, mm9 to mm10) using chain files that map aligned regions between assemblies. The UCSC liftOver tool is the standard utility for this task.

min_match.description: Minimum fraction of bases in the input region that must remap to the target assembly

default_conservative.when: Standard coordinate conversion for point features (SNPs, peaks, binding sites)
default_conservative.why: Default value ensures high confidence that the remapped region corresponds to the same genomic location. 95% of bases must map successfully. Appropriate for most coordinate conversion tasks.

relaxed_for_larger_regions.when: Converting larger genomic regions (>10kb) or regions near assembly gaps
relaxed_for_larger_regions.why: Large regions are more likely to span assembly changes (gap closures, sequence additions). A relaxed minMatch allows partial remapping while still ensuring the majority of the region maps successfully.

stringent_for_clinical.when: Clinical variant annotation where coordinate accuracy is critical
stringent_for_clinical.why: For clinical applications, incorrect coordinate mapping could lead to wrong variant interpretation. Use the most stringent threshold and manually review any unmapped or partially mapped variants.

common_mistakes: Setting minMatch to 0.0 which causes segfaults
Not checking the unmapped output file - it contains regions that failed to convert
Using minMatch=1.0 and losing too many regions unnecessarily

problematic_regions.description: Genomic regions where liftOver is unreliable or fails

centromeres_and_telomeres.value_or_range: Expect high failure rate; pre-exclude or handle separately
centromeres_and_telomeres.when: Converting coordinates in or near centromeric/telomeric regions
centromeres_and_telomeres.why: Centromeres and telomeres are poorly assembled in most genome builds and differ substantially between assemblies. Unconvertible regions are mainly around telomeres and centromeres. These regions have repetitive sequences that cannot be reliably mapped between assemblies.

segmental_duplications.value_or_range: Higher error rate; validate lifted coordinates manually
segmental_duplications.when: Converting coordinates in segmentally duplicated regions
segmental_duplications.why: Conversion-unstable positions are associated with segmental duplications. Duplicated sequences can map to multiple locations, leading to ambiguous coordinate conversion.

assembly_gaps.when: Regions overlapping assembly gaps in either the source or target assembly
assembly_gaps.why: Gaps represent unsequenced or unresolved regions. Coordinates overlapping gaps may remap incorrectly or not at all. Pre-excluding problematic positions prior to conversion results in stable, reliable conversions.

indels_and_structural_variants.value_or_range: Use BCFtools/liftover for variants instead of UCSC liftOver for BED
indels_and_structural_variants.when: Converting variant calls (VCF format) between assemblies
indels_and_structural_variants.why: Indels/duplications are more complicated and error-prone than SNVs due to variant size and sequence context. BCFtools/liftover has the lowest rate of variants being dropped and an order of magnitude fewer indels incorrectly converted compared to alternatives.

common_mistakes: Not pre-filtering known problematic regions (centromeres, gaps, segmental duplications) before liftOver
Using UCSC liftOver for VCF variant files instead of variant-aware tools like BCFtools/liftover or Picard LiftoverVcf
Not checking liftOver success rate and investigating unmapped regions
Assuming liftOver works for cross-species coordinate conversion (it is designed for same-species assembly updates only)

chain_file_selection.description: Selection of the correct chain file for coordinate conversion

same_species_assembly_update.value_or_range: Use official UCSC chain files (e.g., hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz)
same_species_assembly_update.when: Converting between different assemblies of the same species
same_species_assembly_update.why: UCSC provides pre-computed chain files for common assembly conversions. These are generated from whole-genome alignments and are the standard resource.

reverse_conversion.value_or_range: Use the reverse chain file (e.g., hg38ToHg19.over.chain.gz)
reverse_conversion.when: Converting from a newer assembly back to an older one
reverse_conversion.why: Forward and reverse chain files are not symmetric. Always use the chain file matching the direction of conversion. The reverse chain is NOT simply the inverse of the forward chain.

common_mistakes: Using the wrong direction chain file (e.g., hg38ToHg19 when converting hg19 to hg38)
Using outdated chain files that don't incorporate recent assembly patches
Attempting cross-species liftOver with same-species chain files or vice versa

genomic_coordinate_liftover.best_practice_notes: Always check the unmapped output file and report the conversion success rate. Pre-exclude regions overlapping centromeres, telomeres, assembly gaps, and segmental duplications for cleaner conversions. For variant data (VCF), use BCFtools/liftover instead of UCSC liftOver. The minMatch parameter controls coverage (how much of the region maps), not sequence identity. Use the correct direction chain file. For clinical/diagnostic applications, manually review all conversions and use stringent minMatch (0.95+). LiftOver is designed for same-species assembly conversion only.
